PortSwigger - API Testing Notes

Notes on API testing, finding vulnerabilities, mass assignment, server-side parameter pollution.

PortSwigger — API Testing Notes

Goal: Find vulnerabilities in APIs that the website frontend doesn’t fully use. Think of an API as a waiter — you send requests, it fetches/updates data. If the waiter doesn’t check who you are or what you’re allowed to order, that’s a bug.

0. What Even Is API Testing?

An API (Application Programming Interface) lets software talk to each other. When you click “Update Email” on a website, behind the scenes it’s doing something like:

PATCH /api/user/wiener
{ "email": "new@email.com" }

API testing = intercepting and abusing those requests.

1. Reconnaissance — Find the Attack Surface First

Before you hack anything, you need to know what endpoints exist.

1.1 Find API Documentation

Developers write docs so other devs can use the API. If exposed, it’s goldmine for attackers.

Common doc paths to check:

/api
/api/docs
/api/swagger/v1
/swagger/index.html
/openapi.json
/api/redoc
/v1/api-docs

Example: You find /api/swagger/v1/users/123 — now also try:

  • /api/swagger/v1
  • /api/swagger
  • /api

Burp Tip: Use Burp Scanner to crawl OpenAPI/Swagger docs automatically. Or use the OpenAPI Parser BApp.

1.2 Find Hidden Endpoints Manually

Even without docs, you can find endpoints by:

  • Watching the Proxy > HTTP History tab in Burp while using the app normally
  • Looking for patterns like /api/, /v1/, /v2/ in URLs
  • Reading JavaScript files — they often contain API calls the UI never shows you

Example JS snippet you might find:

fetch('/api/admin/users/delete', { method: 'POST' })

→ That delete endpoint might not be linked anywhere in the UI but still works!

1.3 Fuzz for Hidden Endpoints

Once you find one endpoint, fuzz similar paths using Burp Intruder.

Example: You know /api/user/update exists. Fuzz the last part:

/api/user/§update§

Wordlist ideas: delete, add, admin, list, export, reset, debug

2. Interact with Endpoints — Find What They Accept

After finding endpoints, figure out how they work:

2.1 Test All HTTP Methods

APIs often have the same endpoint doing different things per method:

Method Typical Use
GET Read data
POST Create data
PUT Replace data
PATCH Update data
DELETE Delete data

Try sending OPTIONS to see what methods are allowed:

OPTIONS /api/user/wiener HTTP/1.1

Response might say: Allow: GET, POST, DELETE

If DELETE is allowed but the frontend never shows a delete button — test it!

2.2 Switch Content Types

If the API only accepts JSON, try XML or form data. Sometimes different parsers have different bugs.

# Original
Content-Type: application/json
{ "username": "wiener" }

# Try switching to
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
username=wiener

3. Finding Hidden Parameters

This is where it gets juicy.

3.1 Compare GET vs POST Responses

Classic example from PortSwigger labs:

You send GET /api/checkout and get back:

{
  "chosen_discount": { "percentage": 0 },
  "chosen_products": [{ "name": "Jacket", "price": 133700 }]
}

But when you POST /api/checkout to actually buy, you only send:

{
  "chosen_products": [{ "product_id": "1", "quantity": 1 }]
}

Spot the difference? chosen_discount is in the GET response but missing from the POST.

→ Try adding it to your POST request!

3.2 Fuzz for Hidden Parameters with Burp

Use Intruder or the Param Miner BApp to guess hidden parameter names.

POST /api/user/update
{ "§hidden_param§": "test" }

Common hidden params to look for: isAdmin, role, debug, internal, discount, price, balance

4. Mass Assignment Vulnerability

What it is: The server blindly maps ALL user input to internal object fields — including ones that shouldn’t be user-controlled.

Simple analogy: You fill out a form with only Name and Email. But the server’s “User” object also has isAdmin. If the server binds everything you send to the object without filtering, you can just add isAdmin: true to your request.

How to find it:

  1. Do a GET request — see what fields the response contains
  2. Do a POST/PATCH with those extra fields added

Example:

Step 1 — GET response reveals extra fields:

GET /api/users/123
{
  "id": 123,
  "email": "user@example.com",
  "isAdmin": false
}

Step 2 — PATCH to update email, but add isAdmin:

PATCH /api/users/123
{
  "email": "new@email.com",
  "isAdmin": true
}

Step 3 — If the server accepts this → you’re now admin.

Mitigation (for devs): Use an allowlist of fields that users can modify. Never auto-bind all request fields.

5. Server-Side Parameter Pollution (SSPP)

What it is: The website takes your input and uses it in an internal API request (one you can’t see directly). If it doesn’t sanitize your input, you can inject extra parameters into that internal request.

Think of it like: You shout an order at a middleman who relays it to the kitchen. If the middleman doesn’t filter what you say, you can sneak extra instructions.

5.1 Query String Injection

Target URL: https://site.com/login?username=carlos

Internally, the server makes: GET /api/private?username=carlos&publicProfile=true

Your attack: Add &admin=true to your username:

username=carlos%26admin%3Dtrue

(URL-encoded &admin=true)

Internally becomes: GET /api/private?username=carlos&admin=true&publicProfile=true

5.2 Truncate the Internal Request with #

Use # (URL-encoded as %23) to truncate the internal query string:

username=carlos%23foo

Internally: GET /api/private?username=carlos#foo&publicProfile=true

Everything after # gets dropped — the publicProfile=true check is bypassed!

How to detect SSPP — inject test characters and watch behavior:

Inject Watch For
%26foo%3Dbar (&foo=bar) Parameter shows up in response or different behavior
%23foo (#foo) Request truncated — different response
%3Dfoo (=foo) Parameter value changed
foo%3Dbar via path Reflected in an error or response

6. Quick Attack Checklist

[ ] Find API docs (swagger, /api, /openapi.json)
[ ] Browse app in Burp, watch HTTP History for /api/ calls
[ ] Read JavaScript files for hidden endpoint URLs
[ ] Test all HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS)
[ ] Switch content types (JSON → XML → form-data)
[ ] Compare GET and POST bodies — look for extra fields
[ ] Add fields from GET response into POST/PATCH requests (mass assignment)
[ ] Fuzz endpoint paths (/api/user/update → /api/user/delete)
[ ] Fuzz parameter names (Param Miner BApp)
[ ] Inject &, =, # into string params (SSPP)
[ ] Try accessing other users' resources (IDOR / BOLA)
[ ] Try privilege escalation via isAdmin, role parameters

7. OWASP API Top 10 (Quick Reference)

# Vulnerability What It Means
1 Broken Object Level Auth (BOLA) Access other users’ data via object IDs
2 Broken Authentication Weak/missing auth on endpoints
3 Broken Object Property Level Auth Read/write fields you shouldn’t (mass assignment)
4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption No rate limiting → DoS or cost abuse
5 Broken Function Level Auth Regular user accessing admin endpoints
6 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows Abuse of business logic (e.g. fake discounts)
7 SSRF Server makes requests to internal services
8 Security Misconfiguration Debug mode on, verbose errors, etc.
9 Improper Inventory Management Old/forgotten API versions still running
10 Unsafe Consumption of APIs Trusting 3rd-party API responses blindly

8. Key Burp Tools for API Testing

Tool Use Case
Proxy > HTTP History Watch all API traffic while browsing
Repeater Manually tweak and resend requests
Intruder Fuzz endpoints and parameters
Scanner Crawl and audit Swagger/OpenAPI docs
Param Miner (BApp) Find hidden/undocumented parameters
OpenAPI Parser (BApp) Parse and test API specs automatically

9. Real Lab Walkthroughs (Summary)

Lab: Exploiting API via Documentation

  1. Log in, update email → Burp catches PATCH /api/user/wiener
  2. Browse to /api → Swagger UI shows all endpoints
  3. Find DELETE /api/user/{username} in docs
  4. Send DELETE /api/user/carlos → Done

Lab: Mass Assignment

  1. Add jacket to cart → POST /api/checkout
  2. GET /api/checkout response has "chosen_discount": {"percentage": 0}
  3. Add that field to the POST body with "percentage": 100
  4. Buy the jacket for $0

Lab: SSPP in Query String

  1. Forget password for administrator
  2. Fuzz the username field with %26admin%3Dtrue, %23foo, etc.
  3. Observe changes in response messages — detect truncation or parameter injection
  4. Exploit to change reset token behavior

10. Tips & Tricks

  • Always check older API versions: /v1/, /v2/ — older ones often have fewer protections
  • Error messages are gold: 400 Bad Request: field 'isAdmin' is read-only — you just found a hidden field!
  • Read JS files: Use Ctrl+F in browser DevTools to search for /api/ in JS
  • Content-type matters: Try application/xml even if the API “only accepts JSON” — parsers differ
  • BOLA = IDOR for APIs: If you see /api/orders/1234, try /api/orders/1235
